newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Amnesty cautions against Seoul student crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty cautions against Seoul student crackdown.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International on Thursday urged South Korea not to arrest people with leftist ideology as Seoul stepped up a crackdown on a pro-North Korean student body.

State prosecutors said that on Friday they would start questioning more than 600 active members of the banned student group, Hanchongryon, which the government maintains takes orders from Pyongyang, unless they quit the organisation.
The militant group has admitted responsibility for the torture killing of a suspected police spy in June.

"We do not condone student violence. But the confrontation with Hanchongryon has led to a more general crackdown, resulting in the arrests of students and former students for peaceful activities and on charges unrelated to the demonstrations," Amnesty International said.

The London-based human rights group said at least 240 students had been arrested since late May when Hanchongryon organised violent street protests to demand the resignation of President Kim Young-sam.
Hanchongryon has also called for the reunification of the Korean peninsula under a formula suggested by communist North Korea.

"The authorities appear to have deliberately confused the public's fear of North Korea with public concern about student violence and have used this to justify increased use of the National Security Law," Amnesty said.
The law, which calls for the maximum penalty of death by hanging, prohibits all activities praising or benefiting North Korea.

"The South Korean authorities should not use the National Security Law to arrest anyone who is simply deemed to be an ideological threat to the state in the run-up to the presidential election in December," Amnesty said.
Human rights groups have said South Korea's ruling camp has often played up threats from communist North Korea in a bid to garner conservative votes.

"The government is not misusing the National Security Law," said a senior information ministry official in Seoul. "We cannot tolerate any violence or the ideology driving students to streets for violence."
The government last month gave Hanchongryon members until the end of July to make public their withdrawal from the militant group, warning them of arrest otherwise.
State prosecutors said a total of 121 of 206 Hanchongryon-affiliated student councils have so far denounced their membership.

Police have arrested three Hanchongryon activists over the fatal beating of Lee Suk, a factory worker, whose badly bruised body was delivered to a hospital last month. More than 200 Hanchongryon members have also been arrested for violence.

A police autopsy showed Lee died as a direct result of the battering by students during a lengthy interrogation aimed at extracting a confession that he was a spy. His wrists were tied with rope during the beating.

Last August, more than 3,000 students were arrested after riot police stormed a Seoul campus to end seven days of Hanchongryon occupation of lecture buildings. A total of 151 students were later jailed.
